name: Stonewall National Monument
author: author-D-2026-10-17
summary:
Stonewall National Monument is a 7.7-acre site in Greenwich Village, New York City: the 0.12-acre Christopher Park, donated by the city, together with the privately owned Stonewall Inn across the street and the surrounding streets and sidewalks. West of 6th Avenue the street grid is a relic of the 18th century, narrow streets meeting at odd angles; in June 1969 that labyrinth helped demonstrators who knew the neighborhood evade riot-control police who were not from the local precinct. [1]

At about 1:15 a.m. on June 28, 1969, undercover police raided the Stonewall Inn, by then one of the city’s most popular LGBTQ bars. Police told customers — many of them transgender women and drag performers, the foundation document says — that anyone who refused to show identification would have to go into a bathroom where police could verify their sex; the patrons refused. The crowd outside shouted “Gay Power!”, and as it grew angrier the officers retreated into the bar and locked themselves inside; 13 people were arrested. Protests continued nightly in Christopher Park and the nearby streets through July 3. [1]

President Barack Obama proclaimed the monument on June 24, 2016; the Stonewall Inn, Christopher Park and parts of the neighborhood had been a National Historic Landmark since 2000. The proclamation calls the uprising a watershed moment for LGBT civil rights and a transformative event in the nation’s civil rights movement, on par with Seneca Falls in 1848 and the 1965 Selma-to-Montgomery march, and describes the nation’s march toward equality and respect for LGBT people as not yet finished. [1] [1]

lgbtq.html:
Through the 1960s, the park brochure says, almost everything about living openly as a lesbian, gay, bisexual or transgender person was a violation of law, rule or policy (the foundation document says this of the years before 1960). In New York people were arrested for same-sex dancing or kissing or for wearing clothes of the perceived opposite gender; police raided bars for serving “homosexuals.” By the 1960s Christopher Park drew LGBTQ youth, many of whom had run away from or been kicked out of their homes. [1] [1] [1]

The park brochure names street kids among the first to fight, and Marsha P. Johnson, one of the most outspoken members of the city’s transgender community, among the first to fight back. With Sylvia Rivera she co-founded STAR, the Street Transvestite Action Revolutionaries, in the early 1970s. Within a year, the 2016 proclamation records, the number of LGBT organizations in the country grew from around 50 to at least 1,500. [1] [1]

women.html: Barbara Gittings organized the New York chapter of the Daughters of Bilitis and in the 1960s organized some of the first protests against the federal ban on employing homosexuals; she helped lobby until the American Psychiatric Association declassified homosexuality as a mental illness in 1973. The New York Daughters of Bilitis joined the Mattachine Society and Philadelphia’s Janus Society to picket Independence Hall on July 4, 1965, and on four successive July 4ths, under a strict dress code meant to present homosexuals as “presentable and employable.” Inside the Stonewall Inn, the foundation document notes, only a very small number of lesbians were among the patrons; in later commemorations, it says, butch lesbians were among the more marginalized members of the community who claimed their place. [1] [1]
